text: Across interviews, Peter Steinberger presents AI building as parallel delegation with closed-loop testing, while explicitly warning inexperienced users to wait before running highly privileged agents.
OpenClaw has unusually large and sustained open-source attention, reaching 383,370 GitHub stars and 80,530 forks by 2026-07-18.
Community evaluation is polarized: users report concrete automation value, while others report setup burden, bugs, cost and security concerns.
Messaging channels reduce the interaction barrier for ordinary users, but they do not reduce the trust, permission and sandboxing complexity of an action-taking agent.
The phrase I ship code I do not read is an incomplete summary of a workflow that shifts verification toward tests, agents and rapid feedback loops rather than eliminating verification.
OpenClaw officially supports one user or trust boundary per gateway and does not treat a shared tool-enabled agent as isolation between mutually untrusted users.
The first 100 public OpenClaw advisories returned by GitHub include 46 high and 50 medium severity entries, evidence of both a broad attack surface and active disclosure and hardening.
Unit 42 found five unblocked malicious ClawHub skills from February through May; OpenClaw removed them and banned the reported accounts.
Agent safety cannot be reduced to isolated filters because memory, plugins, external content, planning and execution compose into cross-stage risks.
The startup slop dispute is evidence of a community norm conflict over authorship, disclosure and attention, not independent proof that Peter Steinberger writing was either good or bad.
OpenClaw Foundation formally launched as a 501(c)(3) nonprofit with a full-time team in July 2026, fulfilling the structural part of the February foundation promise.

The Foundation existence does not by itself prove long-term neutrality because Peter retains technical authority while employed by OpenAI and external analysts still question independence and sponsor influence.

Peter Steinberger main contribution is product and harness innovation: he made action-taking agents visible and usable through integrations, tools and feedback loops rather than inventing a new foundation model.
The central lesson is to study Peter high-agency building method as an experiment, while designing safe delegation, explicit permissions and recovery mechanisms as first-class product features.

Peter reduced line-by-line reading but did not claim to abandon system understanding; he tracks components, structure and overall design and builds verification loops around agent-callable interfaces.
